mcqs.question: What is the primary job of an on-call engineer when a page fires?
options: Triage quickly — assess how bad it is and whether to escalate — not necessarily fix the entire problem alone
Personally resolve the root cause before contacting anyone else
Wait for a second alert to confirm the first one wasn't a false positive
Immediately write the postmortem document before investigating
mcqs.explanation: On-call is fundamentally about fast triage and appropriate escalation, not solo heroics — knowing when you're out of your depth and pulling in help is as much the job as fixing things directly. Waiting for confirmation wastes response time, and postmortems come after resolution, not before investigation.

mcqs.question: Why does getting the severity call right in the first few minutes of an incident matter so much?
options: Severity only affects which dashboard the incident appears on
It determines everything downstream — how many people get paged, whether a status page update goes out, and how much follow-up process applies
Severity is purely a historical record with no effect on the live response
Lower severity incidents don't require any documentation at all
mcqs.explanation: Severity drives the entire shape of the response in real time: paging scope, stakeholder communication, and how much process follows. Getting it wrong early either under-mobilizes a real emergency or over-escalates a minor blip, both of which cost time and trust; it's far more than a label or a record.

mcqs.question: Why does the incident commander role explicitly not need to be the person actively debugging the issue?
options: Because commanders are never technical enough to understand the debugging
Because only responders are allowed to touch production systems
Because commanders must have more seniority than any responder
Because the commander's job is coordination and decision-making under uncertainty, which is a different task from diagnosis and is degraded by trying to do both at once
mcqs.explanation: Separating coordination from diagnosis means the best debugger isn't also stuck making severity calls and fielding stakeholder questions, and the commander isn't distracted trying to solve the technical problem themselves. Seniority and technical skill aren't the deciding factor — role clarity under pressure is.

mcqs.question: A deploy correlates with the start of a live outage, but the team hasn't yet confirmed exactly why the new code causes the failure. What's the right move?
options: Wait until the mechanism is fully understood before taking any action, per standard debugging discipline
Roll back the deploy now to stop customer impact, and investigate the mechanism afterward with the pressure off
Ignore the deploy correlation since correlation isn't causation
Restart all affected processes first to gather fresh diagnostic data
mcqs.explanation: During an active incident, mitigating impact takes priority over fully understanding the cause — a rollback that stops customer pain in minutes beats a root-cause fix that takes much longer to develop, even though it doesn't explain the mechanism yet. Waiting for full understanding prolongs the outage, and restarting processes risks destroying the evidence needed for the later investigation.

mcqs.question: A team's on-call engineers frequently debug alone for hours on issues beyond their expertise before anyone else gets involved. What does this suggest?
options: The escalation policy or culture doesn't make it easy or acceptable to pull in help early
The team's alerting thresholds are too sensitive and page too often
The team has too many people in its on-call rotation
The engineers involved lack sufficient technical skill for on-call duty
mcqs.explanation: Solo debugging for hours without escalating is the signature of under-escalation — no clear, low-friction path to pull in help, or a culture that discourages asking. Overly sensitive alerting causes the opposite problem (alert fatigue from too much paging), and this pattern isn't primarily about skill or rotation size.

mcqs.question: An on-call engineer has been investigating a live outage for 45 minutes, absorbed in understanding the root cause, with impact still ongoing. What check-in question would have caught this earlier?
options: "Have we identified the exact root cause yet?"
"Do we have a mitigation we could ship right now, even an imperfect one?"
"Who should write the postmortem once this is resolved?"
"Should we schedule a retrospective meeting for next week?"
mcqs.explanation: The framing gap in this failure mode is chasing root cause while impact continues; a fixed check-in that asks specifically about an available mitigation — not about understanding — is what redirects effort toward stopping the bleeding first. The other questions are either premature (root cause, postmortem authorship) or irrelevant to ending the active impact.
